analysis.one_liner: Allows the government to negotiate lower Medicare prescription drug prices.
analysis.headline: The bill to let Medicare negotiate drug prices was referred to two House committees and never advanced before the 112th Congress ended in January 2013.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal law currently bars the Health and Human Services Secretary from interfering in the price deals drug makers strike with Medicare's private drug plans — a rule often called the 'non-interference' provision. This bill would repeal it, letting the Secretary negotiate Medicare drug prices directly, and require that any savings stay within the Medicare program. It was introduced late in the 112th Congress, referred to two House committees, and received no further action before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries would benefit if negotiated prices lowered their prescription drug costs, and taxpayers would benefit if Medicare paid less for covered drugs. The bill requires that any savings be used only for Medicare purposes [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the 'non-interference' provision in Medicare Part D, which currently prohibits the HHS Secretary from interfering in negotiations between drug manufacturers and pharmacies and Part D plan sponsors, and from requiring a particular formulary or price structure for Part D drugs [S2] [S3].
Removes the legal bar on the Secretary negotiating prices for Part D covered drugs, taking effect for plan years beginning January 1, 2013 [S3].
Requires that any savings to Medicare from the change be used only for purposes of the Medicare program, rather than for other federal spending [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Pharmaceutical manufacturers would bear the cost, since allowing government negotiation of Medicare drug prices could reduce the prices they charge the program and their resulting revenue.

drawbacks.text: Supporters of the non-interference provision have argued that government negotiation could lead to restrictive formularies or reduced access to some drugs, since price negotiation would be paired with more federal control over which drugs are covered — a tradeoff the bill's repeal of the formulary restriction would make possible [S2].
The bill was introduced with only two cosponsors and no companion action in the Senate, giving it no realistic path to passage in the short time remaining in the 112th Congress [S4] [S5].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would address one of the largest federal purchases of prescription drugs, potentially lowering Medicare drug costs for seniors and taxpayers, while the main cost falls on drug manufacturers' Medicare revenue. Its central weakness was political timing and support, not design: it arrived two months before a Congress ended, with minimal cosponsorship, and would likely have faced industry-backed resistance had it advanced.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means committees, then to a Health subcommittee, and neither committee ever took it up before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Tammy Baldwin introduced the bill on September 13, 2012 [S1] [S5].
It was referred that day to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and the Ways and Means Committee [S5].
The next day it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Health Subcommittee, where action stopped [S5].
The bill attracted two cosponsors, both Democrats [S4].
No further action was recorded before the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013, so the bill died without a committee vote or floor action [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers came out ahead: the legal prohibition on Medicare negotiating drug prices remained in force, preserving the prices they charge the program. Medicare beneficiaries did not get the negotiating authority the bill proposed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Drug manufacturers kept the status quo

against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no action before the Congress ended

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote, so no roll-call positions exist; its sponsor and both cosponsors were Democrats, and the House Republican majority controlled the committees that took no action [S4] [S5].

industries.note: The bill repeals the Part D non-interference provision that bars the government from negotiating Medicare drug prices, potentially reducing what manufacturers are paid by Medicare. For ordinary people, lower Medicare drug spending means lower premiums, out-of-pocket costs, or taxpayer burden; the industry's interest runs against that.

industries.industry: Medicare Part D private drug plans
industries.note: Plan sponsors currently negotiate directly with manufacturers under a system where the government cannot interfere; direct federal negotiation could reshape their role in setting formularies and reimbursement. Their interest is in preserving the existing structure rather than in lowering prices for beneficiaries.
